goals: Draw and label the external and internal structure of a bean seed and a maize grain
State the function of each part of the seed
Tabulate the differences between monocot and dicot seeds

slides.heading: Seeds: Structure and Germination
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a seed is made of, in a bean and in a maize grain.

nodes.label: Seed: seed coat, embryo, food store

visual.alt: Flow from the ovule through fertilisation to a seed with a seed coat, an embryo and a food store

slides.narration: After fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed. Every seed has the same three jobs to do: protect a tiny new plant, feed it, and wait until conditions are right. We start by opening a bean seed.

slides.heading: A bean seed: outside and inside
slides.body_md: A bean has **two cotyledons** and no separate food store. It is a **dicot** seed.

slides.narration: From outside you see the seed coat, a scar called the hilum where the seed hung from the fruit, and a tiny hole, the micropyle. Inside are two thick cotyledons and the embryo with its plumule and radicle.

slides.heading: Parts of a bean seed and what they do

rows: Protects the embryo; keeps out germs and prevents drying
Scar left where the seed was attached to the fruit
Tiny pore; takes in water and lets the radicle come out

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a bean seed and the function of each

slides.narration: The seed coat protects. The micropyle lets water in. The two cotyledons are the food store. The embryo itself is the plumule, which becomes the shoot, and the radicle, which becomes the root.

slides.heading: A maize grain
slides.body_md: A maize grain is really a **fruit with one seed**. It has **one cotyledon**, the **scutellum**, and a large **endosperm**.

visual.alt: A maize grain in long section with its parts labelled

slides.narration: In a maize grain the fruit wall and seed coat are joined. Most of the grain is endosperm, the food store. At one side is the embryo, with a shield-like scutellum, a plumule inside a sheath called the coleoptile, and a radicle inside a sheath called the coleorhiza.

slides.heading: Parts of a maize grain and what they do

rows: Large store of food, mainly starch
The single cotyledon; passes food from the endosperm to the embryo
Shoot; the coleoptile protects it as it pushes up
Root; the coleorhiza protects it as it pushes down

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a maize grain and the function of each

slides.narration: The endosperm holds the food. The scutellum passes that food to the embryo. The coleoptile is a sheath that guards the young shoot, and the coleorhiza is a sheath that guards the young root.

slides.heading: Quick check: the shield
slides.body_md: Which part of a maize grain is its single cotyledon?
slides.narration: Its name sounds like a shield.

slides.heading: Dicot and monocot seeds compared

rows: In the cotyledons; no separate endosperm in a mature seed
Fruit wall joined to the seed coat

visual.alt: Table comparing a dicot seed with a monocot seed in five features

slides.narration: Count the cotyledons first. Dicots have two, monocots have one. A bean keeps its food in its cotyledons, while maize keeps it in a separate endosperm. Only maize has the two protective sheaths, the coleoptile and the coleorhiza.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting cotyledons
slides.body_md: A bag holds 25 bean seeds and 25 maize grains. How many cotyledons are there altogether?
bullets: Step 1: a bean seed has 2 cotyledons, so 25 × 2 = **50**.
Step 2: a maize grain has 1 cotyledon, so 25 × 1 = **25**.

visual.alt: Worked table: fifty bean cotyledons, twenty-five maize cotyledons and seventy-five in all

slides.narration: Count by kind of seed. Twenty-five beans with two cotyledons each give fifty. Twenty-five maize grains with one cotyledon each give twenty-five. Together there are seventy-five cotyledons.

slides.narration: Count the cotyledons.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming the seed from clues
slides.body_md: A student soaks a seed and splits it into two thick halves with a tiny shoot between them. There is no separate food store and no sheath around the shoot.
bullets: Step 1: two thick halves are **two cotyledons**.
Step 2: no separate endosperm and no sheaths point away from maize.
Step 3: so it is a **dicot seed**, like the **bean**.

visual.alt: Worked table: clues in the soaked seed and what each points to

slides.narration: Work from the clues. Two thick halves mean two cotyledons. No separate food store and no sheaths mean it is not like maize. So the seed is a dicot, like a bean.

slides.heading: Why each part matters

rows: Seed coat (and fruit wall in maize)

visual.alt: Table matching the needs of a young plant to the seed part that meets each

slides.narration: Think of the seed as a packed lunch for a journey. The coat is the wrapper, the micropyle is the way in for water, the food store is the lunch, and the plumule and radicle are the traveller.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Bean: two cotyledons, plumule, radicle, hilum, micropyle, seed coat.
Maize: one cotyledon (scutellum), endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza.
Dicot: two cotyledons. Monocot: one cotyledon.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing a bean seed and a maize grain

slides.narration: To recap. A bean is a dicot seed with two cotyledons that store food. Maize is a monocot grain with one cotyledon, the scutellum, and a large endosperm. Only maize has the coleoptile and coleorhiza.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In a labelled diagram show the **hilum and micropyle** from outside and the **plumule and radicle** inside.
Do not call the **scutellum** the endosperm: it is the **cotyledon**.
In a table of differences, give a **matching point** for each seed.
Use **ruled lines** that touch the part.
slides.narration: Exam tips. In diagrams, draw the hilum and micropyle, and the plumule and radicle. Never confuse the scutellum with the endosperm. In a table of differences, write a matching point for each seed. And use neat ruled lines.

goals: Describe the stages of germination of a bean seed and a maize grain
Distinguish hypogeal from epigeal germination with examples
Design an experiment to show that water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are needed

slides.heading: Germination
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how a resting seed becomes a seedling, and what it needs.

visual.alt: Flow from water taken in to radicle emerging, plumule growing and a seedling

slides.narration: A dry seed is alive but resting. Germination is the growth of the embryo into a seedling. It begins when the seed takes in water, and the radicle is the first part to come out.

slides.heading: Stages of germination of a bean

rows: The seed takes in water through the micropyle and swells
The radicle emerges first and grows down as the root
The hypocotyl lengthens, bends into an arch and pulls the cotyledons above the soil
The plumule opens into the first leaves; the cotyledons shrink as their food is used

visual.alt: Table of five stages in the germination of a bean seed

slides.narration: Water comes first and the seed swells. The coat splits. The radicle goes down as the root. Then the hypocotyl arches and drags the cotyledons into the light, and the plumule opens into leaves.

slides.heading: Two ways to germinate
slides.body_md: In **epigeal** germination the **hypocotyl** lengthens; in **hypogeal** germination the **epicotyl** lengthens.

slides.narration: In the bean, the hypocotyl grows long and lifts the cotyledons above the ground. In the pea, the epicotyl grows long and the cotyledons stay in the soil. The word epigeal means above the earth, hypogeal means below.

slides.heading: Epigeal and hypogeal germination

rows: Carried above the soil; may turn green

visual.alt: Table comparing epigeal and hypogeal germination

slides.narration: Ask one question: where do the cotyledons end up? Above the soil means epigeal. Below the soil means hypogeal. Beans are epigeal. Peas, gram and maize are hypogeal.

slides.heading: Quick check: where do the cotyledons end up?
slides.body_md: A seedling lifts its two cotyledons above the soil as the hypocotyl lengthens. This is
slides.narration: Remember the meaning of the word.

slides.heading: Germination of a maize grain

rows: The grain absorbs water and swells
The coleorhiza is pushed out and the radicle breaks through it
The coleoptile grows up through the soil, protecting the plumule
The plumule breaks through the coleoptile and forms leaves
The scutellum passes food from the endosperm to the seedling

visual.alt: Table of five stages in the germination of a maize grain

slides.narration: Maize is hypogeal. The coleorhiza and coleoptile act like protective tips, guarding the root and the shoot as they push through the soil. The scutellum passes food across from the endosperm.

slides.heading: Quick check: the shoot guard
slides.body_md: In a germinating maize grain, the sheath that protects the young shoot is the
slides.narration: It is the sheath for the plumule.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which type, and how long?
slides.body_md: A seed is sown 4 centimetres deep. After germination, the cotyledons stay in the soil and the epicotyl lengthens 2 centimetres each day. Name the type of germination and find the days the shoot needs to reach the surface.
bullets: Step 1: cotyledons stay in the soil and the epicotyl grows, so it is **hypogeal**.
Step 2: days = depth ÷ growth each day = 4 ÷ 2 = **2**.

visual.alt: Worked table: hypogeal germination, four centimetres deep, two centimetres a day, two days to reach the surface

slides.narration: First decide the type. The cotyledons stay below the soil, so it is hypogeal. Then divide the depth by the daily growth. Four divided by two is two days.

slides.heading: Conditions needed for germination

rows: Softens the seed coat, activates enzymes and carries food to the embryo
For respiration, which releases energy for growth
Enzymes work best in warmth; too cold or too hot stops germination

visual.alt: Table of three conditions for germination and why each is needed

slides.narration: A seed needs three things. Water to wake up its enzymes, oxygen for respiration to release energy, and a suitable temperature. Light is not needed by most seeds until the seedling has leaves.

sections.heading: 1. Structure of a bean seed and a maize grain
sections.body_md:
A **seed** is a ripened ovule: a **seed coat**, an **embryo** and a **food store**.

**Bean (dicot) seed**
- **External:** seed coat; **hilum** (scar where the seed was attached); **micropyle** (tiny pore that takes in water and lets the radicle out).
- **Internal:** **two cotyledons** that store food; the **embryo axis** with the **plumule** (future shoot) and **radicle** (future root).

**Maize (monocot) grain**: really a **fruit with one seed**; the fruit wall and seed coat are joined.
- **Endosperm:** large food store (mainly starch).
- **Scutellum:** the single cotyledon; passes food from the endosperm to the embryo.
- **Plumule** inside the **coleoptile** (sheath); **radicle** inside the **coleorhiza** (sheath).

**Diagrams:** draw the bean seed from outside and opened, and the maize grain in long section, with ruled labels.

The part of the embryo that grows into the shoot.
The part of the embryo that grows into the root.
The scar on a seed where it was attached to the fruit.
A tiny pore in the seed coat.

sections.heading: 2. Differences between monocot and dicot seeds
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Dicot seed (bean) | Monocot seed (maize) |
|---|---|---|
| Cotyledons | Two | One (scutellum) |
| Food store | In the cotyledons; no separate endosperm when mature | In a large separate endosperm |
| Covering | Seed coat only | Fruit wall joined to the seed coat |
| Sheaths on the embryo | None | Coleoptile and coleorhiza |
| Germination (examples) | Epigeal (bean) | Hypogeal (maize) |

Books differ on whether to call the bean "non-endospermic" and maize "endospermic"; this chapter follows that usual division. Some dicot seeds (castor) do keep an endosperm, and the germination type is not fixed by the number of cotyledons (broad bean and pea are dicots with hypogeal germination).

key_terms.definition_md: A flowering plant with two cotyledons in its seed.
A flowering plant with one cotyledon in its seed.

sections.heading: 3. Germination; hypogeal and epigeal
sections.body_md:
**Germination** is the growth of the embryo into a seedling.

**Bean:** water enters by the micropyle and the seed swells; the coat splits; the **radicle** emerges first; the **hypocotyl** lengthens, arches and pulls the cotyledons above the soil (**epigeal**); the plumule opens into the first leaves; the cotyledons shrink as their food is used.

**Maize:** the grain swells; the radicle breaks through the **coleorhiza**; the **coleoptile** pushes up with the plumule inside; the plumule breaks out; the **scutellum** passes food from the endosperm. The cotyledon stays in the soil (**hypogeal**).

| | Epigeal | Hypogeal |
|---|---|---|
| Part that lengthens | Hypocotyl | Epicotyl |
| Cotyledons | Carried above the soil | Stay below the soil |
| Examples | Bean, castor, cotton | Pea, gram, maize |

Books differ for "bean": the French (kidney) bean used here is epigeal, while the broad bean is hypogeal.

key_terms.definition_md: The growth of the embryo of a seed into a seedling.
Germination in which the cotyledons are lifted above the soil.
Germination in which the cotyledons stay below the soil.

sections.heading: 4. Conditions for germination and experiments
sections.body_md:
- **Water:** softens the coat, activates enzymes, carries food to the embryo.
- **Oxygen:** for respiration, which releases energy for growth.
- **Suitable temperature:** enzymes work best in warmth; too cold or too hot stops germination.
- Most seeds do not need light to germinate.

**Experiment:** use four tubes with the same kind and number of seeds, changing **one condition at a time**. (1) Dry cotton wool: no water. (2) Seeds under boiled, cooled water with a layer of oil: no oxygen. (3) Moist cotton wool in an ice bath: low temperature. (4) Moist cotton wool at room temperature, open to the air: all conditions (the **control**). Only the control germinates well.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling the **scutellum** the endosperm (it is the cotyledon).
- Forgetting the **hilum and micropyle** in the external view.
- Mixing up **epigeal** (cotyledons above soil, hypocotyl lengthens) with **hypogeal** (below soil, epicotyl lengthens).
- Changing **more than one** condition in an experiment, or leaving out the **control**.
- Naming a condition without a **reason**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two differences or two functions, matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a labelled diagram or three matched points.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: A student splits a soaked seed into two equal halves, each thick with stored food. There is no separate food tissue. The seed is most likely a

options.text_md: dicot seed such as a bean

questions.solution_md: Two food-filled halves are two cotyledons, so it is a dicot seed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which feature is found in a maize grain but not in a bean seed?
questions.solution_md: Only the maize grain has a coleoptile — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In which seed is the main food store a separate tissue outside the cotyledon?
questions.solution_md: Maize stores food in the endosperm, outside the single cotyledon — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A bag holds 25 bean seeds and 25 maize grains. How many cotyledons are there in the 25 bean seeds?
questions.solution_md: $25 \times 2 = 50$ cotyledons.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A maize seed is a monocot seed.

**Reason (R):** A maize grain has two cotyledons.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: maize has one cotyledon, the scutellum — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A dicot seed always has a large separate endosperm when it is ripe.
questions.solution_md: False. A bean stores food in its cotyledons and has no separate endosperm when ripe.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: a seed with two cotyledons.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dicot seed** (dicotyledonous seed).

questions.solution_md: Dicot seed.

questions.stem_md:
Select the correct terms to fill in the blanks: [endosperm, scutellum, cotyledons, coleoptile, plumule, hilum, radicle, micropyle]

A bean seed has two (a) ______ that store food. A maize grain stores its food in the (b) ______, and the single cotyledon of maize is the (c) ______. In maize the sheath around the shoot is the (d) ______, and the part of the embryo that becomes the root is the (e) ______.
questions.solution_md: (a) cotyledons; (b) endosperm; (c) scutellum; (d) coleoptile; (e) radicle.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between a bean seed and a maize grain in the number of cotyledons and the place where food is stored.

answer.model_answer_md: A **bean** has **two cotyledons** and stores food **in the cotyledons**. A **maize grain** has **one cotyledon** (scutellum) and stores food **in the endosperm**.

questions.solution_md: Cotyledon number; food store.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between a monocot seed and a dicot seed.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Monocot seed | Dicot seed |
|---|---|
| **One** cotyledon | **Two** cotyledons |
| Food in a large **endosperm** | Food in the **cotyledons** |
| Embryo has **coleoptile and coleorhiza** | **No** such sheaths |
| Fruit wall **joined** to seed coat (maize) | Seed coat **only** |

questions.solution_md: Cotyledons; food store; sheaths.

questions.stem_md: A seed has one cotyledon, a large endosperm and a coleoptile. Name its type and give one example.

answer.model_answer_md: One cotyledon, a large endosperm and a coleoptile show that it is a **monocot seed**. A familiar example is **maize** (or wheat), whose single cotyledon is the scutellum.

questions.solution_md: Monocot; maize.

questions.stem_md: When a seed germinates, the first part of the embryo to come out of the seed coat is the
questions.solution_md: The radicle emerges first and anchors the seedling — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A gardener sows gram seeds. After germination he sees the shoot but the cotyledons stay under the soil. This is

options.text_md: hypogeal germination, with the epicotyl lengthening
epigeal germination, with the hypocotyl lengthening
epigeal germination, with the epicotyl lengthening
hypogeal germination, with the hypocotyl lengthening

questions.solution_md: Cotyledons that stay below the soil show hypogeal germination, driven by the epicotyl — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the germination of a bean seed, the arch that pulls the cotyledons upward is formed by the
questions.solution_md: The hypocotyl lengthens and arches — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During germination of a maize grain, food reaches the seedling from the endosperm through the
questions.solution_md: The scutellum passes food across — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The cotyledons of a bean seedling turn green and shrivel later. They turn green because they are

options.text_md: carried into the light above the soil and make food for a short time

questions.solution_md: Epigeal cotyledons reach the light and can make some food before shrinking — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The radicle is the first part to emerge from a germinating seed.

**Reason (R):** The young seedling must anchor itself and absorb water from the soil.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the early need for anchorage and water explains why the root comes first — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Maize shows epigeal germination.
questions.solution_md: False. Maize shows hypogeal germination; its cotyledon stays in the soil.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: germination in which the cotyledons remain below the soil.

answer.model_answer_md: **Hypogeal germination.**

questions.solution_md: Hypogeal.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Bean, Castor, Cotton, Pea.

answer.model_answer_md: **Pea**; the others show **epigeal germination**.

questions.solution_md: Pea is hypogeal.

questions.stem_md: The radicle of a germinating seed measures 3 mm on day 1 and 30 mm on day 4. What is its mean growth in millimetres each day over these three days?
questions.solution_md: $(30 - 3) \div 3 = 9$ mm per day.

questions.stem_md: A hypogeal seed is sown 4 cm deep. Its shoot grows 2 cm each day. In how many days does the shoot reach the surface?
questions.solution_md: $4 \div 2 = 2$ days.

questions.stem_md: State two differences between epigeal and hypogeal germination.

answer.model_answer_md: In **epigeal** germination the **hypocotyl lengthens** and the **cotyledons are carried above the soil**. In **hypogeal** germination the **epicotyl lengthens** and the **cotyledons stay below the soil**.

questions.solution_md: Part that lengthens; position of cotyledons.

questions.stem_md: Describe the stages of germination of a bean seed in the correct order.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The seed **takes in water**, swells and the **seed coat splits**.
2. The **radicle emerges first** and grows down as the root.
3. The **hypocotyl arches** and pulls the **cotyledons above the soil**; the **plumule** opens into the first leaves.

questions.solution_md: Water and splitting; radicle; hypocotyl and plumule.

marking_scheme.step: Hypocotyl lifts cotyledons; plumule forms leaves

questions.stem_md: Describe the part played by the coleorhiza, the coleoptile and the scutellum in the germination of maize.

answer.model_answer_md: The **coleorhiza** **protects the radicle** as the root pushes out. The **coleoptile** **protects the plumule** as the shoot pushes up through the soil. The **scutellum** **passes food from the endosperm** to the growing embryo.

questions.solution_md: Coleorhiza protects root; coleoptile protects shoot; scutellum passes food.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between epigeal and hypogeal germination, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Epigeal | Hypogeal |
|---|---|
| **Hypocotyl** lengthens | **Epicotyl** lengthens |
| Cotyledons **above** the soil | Cotyledons **stay below** the soil |
| Example: **bean** (or castor) | Example: **pea, gram or maize** |

questions.solution_md: Part that lengthens; cotyledons; examples.

questions.stem_md: Which set of conditions is needed for most seeds to germinate?

options.text_md: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature

questions.solution_md: Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature are the three conditions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Dry seeds stored in a sealed tin in a cool store do not germinate. The main reason is that

options.text_md: they have no water to start the changes inside the seed

questions.solution_md: Without water the enzymes stay inactive — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Seeds placed on moist cotton wool in a refrigerator germinate very little because

options.text_md: the cotton wool contains no oxygen
the low temperature slows the changes in the seed

questions.solution_md: Too low a temperature slows the enzymes — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a germination experiment with four tubes, the tube with moist cotton wool at room temperature, open to the air, is the
questions.solution_md: It has every condition and is used for comparison — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of four tubes of seeds, which tube shows that oxygen is needed for germination?
questions.solution_md: In Q the oil and boiled water keep air from the seeds — option (d).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Control.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the water used to cover the seeds in an oxygen experiment is boiled and cooled first.

questions.solution_md: Removes dissolved oxygen.

questions.stem_md: State two reasons why water is needed for the germination of a seed.

answer.model_answer_md: Water **softens the seed coat** and **activates the enzymes**; it also **carries food** to the growing embryo.

questions.solution_md: Any two roles of water.

questions.stem_md: Why do germinating seeds need oxygen and a suitable temperature?

answer.model_answer_md: Oxygen is needed for **respiration**, which releases the **energy** for growth. A suitable temperature lets the **enzymes work well**.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen for respiration; temperature for enzymes.

questions.stem_md: Describe how you would show that seeds need water to germinate. Name the control.

answer.model_answer_md: Place the **same number of similar seeds** in two tubes: one on **dry cotton wool** and one on **moist cotton wool**, both at **room temperature in air**. After some days the seeds on the **moist cotton wool (the control)** germinate and those on the dry cotton wool do not.

questions.solution_md: Two tubes, same seeds, only water differs; moist tube is the control.

marking_scheme.step: Same seeds, dry and moist cotton wool
Moist tube is the control, result stated

questions.stem_md:
A nursery assistant has two seeds, X and Y. X has two thick halves and no separate food tissue. Y has one flat cotyledon beside a large starchy tissue, with a sheath around its shoot and another around its root.

(a) Name the type of seed each is and name one example of each. [2]

(b) Name the sheaths of Y and state what each protects. [2]

(c) Tabulate two differences between X and Y apart from the sheaths. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of Y in long section, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** X is a **dicot** seed (bean); Y is a **monocot** grain (maize).

**(b)** The **coleoptile** protects the **plumule**; the **coleorhiza** protects the **radicle**.

**(c)** X has **two** cotyledons, Y **one**; X stores food **in the cotyledons**, Y in the **endosperm**.

**(d)** A grain outline with **endosperm**, **scutellum**, **plumule** in its coleoptile and **radicle** in its coleorhiza. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Dicot bean, monocot maize; coleoptile and coleorhiza; two differences; labelled maize grain.

questions.stem_md:
A student sets up four tubes P, Q, R and S, each with 20 similar seeds. P: dry cotton wool at room temperature. Q: seeds under boiled, cooled water with a layer of oil. R: moist cotton wool in an ice bath. S: moist cotton wool at room temperature, open to the air. After a week 0, 0, 1 and 19 seeds had germinated in P, Q, R and S.

(a) Calculate the percentage of seeds that germinated in R and in S. [2]

(b) Name the condition missing in P and in Q. [2]

(c) Name the control and state why it is needed. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of tube Q, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** R: 1 ÷ 20 × 100 = **5%**. S: 19 ÷ 20 × 100 = **95%**.

**(b)** P lacks **water**; Q lacks **oxygen (air)**.

**(c)** **Tube S** is the control, with all conditions; it is needed to **compare** with the other tubes and show that the seeds were able to germinate.

**(d)** A **test tube** holding **seeds** at the bottom, **boiled, cooled water** above them and a **layer of oil** on top. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: 5% and 95%; water and oxygen; tube S is the control; labelled tube.

questions.stem_md:
A student sows bean seeds and pea seeds in separate pots. After a week she finds the two green seed leaves of the bean seedling above the soil, while in the pea seedling the seed leaves are still in the soil.

(a) Name the type of germination shown by each seedling. [2]

(b) Name the part that lengthens in each seedling to cause the difference. [2]

(c) State which structure comes out of the seed first in both and why it does so. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the bean seedling above the soil, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Bean: **epigeal**. Pea: **hypogeal**.

**(b)** Bean: the **hypocotyl**. Pea: the **epicotyl**.

**(c)** The **radicle**; it **anchors the seedling and absorbs water** from the soil.

**(d)** A seedling with **root** in the soil, the **hypocotyl**, two **cotyledons** above the soil and young **leaves** (plumule); soil level marked. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Epigeal and hypogeal; hypocotyl and epicotyl; radicle anchors; labelled seedling.

questions.stem_md:
Study the diagram of a maize grain in long section. Parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts B and C and state the function of each. [3]

(b) Name the parts D and E and the sheath that protects each. [2]

(c) State the order in which E and D come out when the grain germinates. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a germinating maize grain showing the shoot and the root, with three labels. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** B is the **endosperm**: stores food. C is the **scutellum**: passes food to the embryo.

**(b)** D is the **plumule**, protected by the **coleoptile**. E is the **radicle**, protected by the **coleorhiza**.

**(c)** **E (the radicle)** emerges first, then **D (the plumule)**.

**(d)** A grain with a **root** below, a **coleoptile** and shoot above, and the **endosperm**. Three labels.

questions.solution_md: Endosperm, scutellum; plumule with coleoptile, radicle with coleorhiza; radicle first; labelled seedling.

questions.stem_md:
A student soaks gram seeds overnight. 12 g of dry seeds become 18 g. After germination the radicle measures 3 mm on day 1, 9 mm on day 2, 18 mm on day 3 and 30 mm on day 4.

(a) Calculate the percentage increase in mass of the seeds. [2]

(b) Calculate the mean growth of the radicle each day from day 1 to day 4. [2]

(c) State two ways in which water helps the seed to germinate. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a germinating seed with the radicle emerging, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Gain = 18 − 12 = 6 g; 6 ÷ 12 × 100 = **50%**.

**(b)** (30 − 3) ÷ 3 = **9 mm per day**.

**(c)** Water **softens the seed coat**, **activates the enzymes** and **carries food** to the embryo (any two).

**(d)** A seed with a split **seed coat**, a **cotyledon**, the **radicle** emerging and the **plumule**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: 50%; 9 mm per day; two roles of water; labelled germinating seed.
